sections.html:
Central Virginia's Blue Ridge foothills hold Lynchburg, an independent city on the James River at about 630 feet. Its 49.53 square miles are almost entirely land, and three counties touch it: Amherst to the northeast, Bedford to the west and northwest, and Campbell to the south and southeast.

Population was 79,009 in 2020 and is estimated at 81,347 for 2025, ranking 11th among Virginia cities. City offices, not a county, issue assessments, tax bills and building rules.

The nickname City of Seven Hills comes from College Hill, Garland Hill, Daniel's Hill, Federal Hill, Diamond Hill, White Rock Hill and Franklin Hill. Steep lots bring retaining walls, long driveways and drainage runs that a flat city does not have, so check yours before a buyer does.

The town grew around a ferry that John Lynch, a Quaker, began operating across the river after 1757, and it was incorporated as a city in 1852. Rivermont, Court House Hill and Downtown, the four named hills of Daniel's, Diamond, Federal and Garland, and the Fifth Street, Kemper Street, Lower Basin, Pierce Street and Twelfth Street areas all have local or state historic status.

Expect original wood windows, plaster walls and aging wiring or plumbing in these areas, with repair bills higher than for a recent build. Buyers ask about age first. Before starting any exterior work, check with the city planning office about design review.

Education and manufacturing anchor the area. Nuclear technology, pharmaceuticals and material handling are among the industries, and five schools of higher learning sit in town: Liberty University, the University of Lynchburg, Randolph College, Virginia University of Lynchburg and Central Virginia Community College. The public high schools are E. C. Glass and Heritage.

Campuses nearby mean a share of local houses are rentals, and a landlord weary of turnover can sell the house exactly as it stands.

Cool winters and hot, humid summers: the January average is 35.9 degrees, July is 76.0, and a typical year has 27.4 days at 90 degrees or higher. Seasonal snow averages 11.6 inches but varies widely, and the record winter of 1995 to 1996 dropped 56.8 inches.

Have the roof and heating system inspected before you sell, since heavy winters expose weak ones. Near the James River or a creek? Pull up the flood map and talk to your insurance agent before listing.

Values for every parcel are reset by the City Assessor on a two-year cycle, and the tax roll covers July 1 through June 30 under Chapter 18-48 of the Lynchburg City Code and Title 58.1 of the Virginia Code.

Visit 900 Church Street, Lynchburg, VA 24504, Monday through Friday, 8:30 am to 5 pm, or try the online ParcelViewer for property details and maps. Because rates are set yearly, call the Assessor or the Treasurer's office for the current rate and billing dates.

Lynchburg sits near the geographic center of Virginia. Greater Lynchburg Transit Company runs the local buses and the campus shuttle at Liberty University. Kemper Street Station, at 825 Kemper Street, serves Amtrak and Greyhound, with the Crescent and a Northeast Regional train stopping there. The Northeast Regional connects Lynchburg with Washington and points north. Two Norfolk Southern lines cross in the city, and CSX also has a presence.

A house near the station or the main bus routes can appeal to commuters and students who prefer not to drive.

Closing for cash looks like any Virginia closing minus the lender. Contract signed, title searched by a settlement company, deed recorded by the circuit court clerk. The deed carries a grantor tax of 50 cents per $500 of value, which the seller pays unless the contract moves it, and recording requires the price on the deed's first page. Ask the settlement agent to confirm exact charges.

  • Gather the deed, the tax bill and any payoff statements.
  • Ask the Assessor's Office about the current value on file.
  • Choose a closing date that fits your move.

Most trouble traces back to old houses and steep ground.

  • Old houses in historic districts that need major repairs.
  • Rentals with turnover and unpaid repairs.
  • Inherited houses with out-of-town heirs.
  • Steep lots with drainage and foundation problems.

Selling this way lets you avoid repair haggling and set your own timeline. Some purchases are ours and some go to a vetted cash buyer; the offer reflects condition and title.

Tell us about the house and we respond with a written offer after reviewing photos or visiting. Agree to it, and the settlement company looks for liens, back taxes and filings against the owner before drafting the deed and settlement statement. After an owner's death, expect a request for proof of who may sign.

With no loan to approve, the closing date is yours inside the limits of the title work. Decide by comparing net figures: repairs on an older house, agent fees and months of carrying costs, set against the cash offer. Get a written statement of who pays title charges, and read the settlement statement before signing.

sections.h2: Getting a hillside or historic house ready
sections.html:
Lynchburg's terrain and older streets give buyers' inspectors plenty to examine. A few hours of your own checking beforehand turns an unknown into a known number.

  • Walk the lot after rain and note where water collects or runs toward the house.
  • Look at retaining walls for leaning, cracks or bulging.
  • Check the foundation for stair-step cracks or doors that stick.
  • Find out whether design review applies if you are in a historic district.
  • Locate permits for any renovation, since older houses often carry unpermitted work.

You do not have to repair what you find. Disclosing it plainly lets a buyer price the work, and that candor is what keeps a deal from falling apart after inspection.

sections.h2: Listing or cash: how to choose
sections.html:
If your house is sound and you can wait through a few months of showings, a listing may bring the higher price. If it needs a roof, has a wet foundation or sits in a historic district where work is costly, the repair bill may erase the difference.

Do the arithmetic honestly. Take the likely listing price, subtract the repairs a buyer's lender would demand, the agent's fee and every month of taxes, utilities and insurance until closing, and compare what is left with the cash offer. Whichever number is larger, with the date you need in mind, is your answer.

faqs.a: No county sits above it. Lynchburg is an independent city next to Amherst, Bedford and Campbell counties, and its own offices assess and tax property.

faqs.q: What is the Lynchburg real estate tax rate?
faqs.a: For 2025 to 2026 the City Assessor listed $0.84 per $100 of assessed value. The rate is reset every year, so ask the city what applies now.

faqs.q: How often does Lynchburg reassess property?
faqs.a: Every parcel gets a new value every two years, while transfers and building permits are handled all year long.

faqs.q: Where do I call about my Lynchburg assessment?
faqs.a: Phone the City Assessor's Office at 434-455-3830 or stop by 900 Church Street, Monday through Friday, 8:30 am to 5 pm.

faqs.q: Can I sell a Lynchburg house in a historic district?
faqs.a: Yes. Any house can be sold as is, though design review rules may apply to exterior changes. Ask the city planning office about your block. Virginia's grantor tax of 50 cents per $500 on the deed is usually paid by the seller.
